Īśāna-śivaguru-deva-paddhati
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Also known as Tantrapaddhati, this is an important work of the tantra-group, almost encyclopaedic in character. Apart from the general topics dealt with in the tantra-literature like mantras, it covers several aspects of subjects treated in the आगमस् such as temples, इचोनोग्रफ्य् and ritualistic worship.
It is a voluminous work in 18,000 verses in various metres. They are spread over in four pādas or sections, each having several paṭalas or chapters, the total number being 119.
The following table gives an idea of the work:
Sāmānyapāda—paṭalas 1 to 14;
Mantrapāda—paṭalas 15 to 52;
Kriyāpāda—paṭalas 1 to 30;
Kriyāpāda (contd.)
—paṭalas 31 to 64;
Yogapāda—paṭalas 1 to 3
The first two pādas are called Pūrvārdha and the last two as Uttarārdha.
The Author
At the end of the very first paṭala, in the colophon, the author has mentioned his name as ‘Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra’. Some scholars believe, based on the surname ‘Miśra’, that he belonged to the country of मिथिला (Janakpur in Uttar Pradesh). However, the overwhelming view is that he belonged to the Kerala State.
There are others who consider him as the गुरु of लीलाशुक (before 15th century) the author of the famous work Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta.
This much can be said that he belonged to a long line of शिव-yogis who were very influential during the period 9th to the 11th centuries A. D.
As regards the title of the text, two more have been suggested. They are:
Tantrasāra paddhati and Siddhānta-sāra. They, however, seem to suggest the nature of the work rather than a regular title.
Source Material
The author has quoted 15 earlier writers and 60 works that were current during his times, as authorities.
Some of the authors are: आर्यभट, गौतम, पतञ्जलि, पराशर, Bhojarāja, मय and वसिष्ठ.
The list of 60 works includes many तन्त्रस् and आगमस् like Prapañcasāra and Ajitāgama as also the Bhagavadgītā and पुराणस् like the Kūrma.
Prayogamañjarī (or Mañjarī) of Ravi and Tattvaprakāśa of Bhojadeva have been quoted more often than the others.
From the list of works quoted, one can guess that the author was well conversant not only with the शैवागमस् but also with several other fields of knowledge such as ज्यौतिष, आयुर्वेद, धर्म-śāstras, various Smṛtis, व्याकरण and योग.
It may not be out of place if it is pointed out that the fragrance of the tāntrik and ritualistic aspects of Kerala temples is reflected in this work for obvious reasons.
A BRIEF SUMMARY OF THE WORK
1. Sāmānyapāda
Paṭala 1 (91 verses)
This is an introductory section. Definition of the term ‘mantra’ and evolution of the 50 letters of the alphabet as the basic units is the subject.
Paṭala 2 (133 verses)
Several concepts like śaktis and kalās commonly dealt with in the तन्त्रस् are enumerated here.
Paṭala 3 (92 verses)
It describes how each of the letters of the alphabet inscribed in a यन्त्र (mystical diagram) has its own form and colour, a knowledge of which is absolutely necessary.
Paṭala 4 (40 verses)
It deals with the general classification of mantras as स्त्री (feminine), pumān (masculine) and ṣaṇḍa (neuter) and the appropriate endings like स्वाहा, and namaḥ.
Paṭala 5 (81 verses)
Six ways of using a मन्त्र in japa—like pallava, योग and sampuṭaka—are described here.
Paṭala 6 (160 verses)
This deals with varieties of अग्नि-kuṇḍas (scrificial pits) and maṇḍalas (esoteric diagrams). The shapes described are identical for both purposes.
Paṭala 7 (37 verses)
Sacrificial vessels like sruk and sruva are described here.
Paṭala 8 (129 verses)
Three kinds of पूजा or ritualistic worship of gods and the various steps involved as आवाहन (inviting), अर्घ्य and pādya (water for washing the hands and feet) are explained in detail.
Paṭala 9 (188 verses)
Bath in water with Vedic mantras and by smearing with भस्म or holy ash—this is called āgneyasnāna (bath by fire)—are described here.
Paṭala 10 (41 verses)
Certain purificatory processes involving the five elements of the body through प्राणायाम and some internal meditations are given here.
Paṭala 11 (71 verses)
This paṭala deals with Vāstupūjā and the worship of the वास्तुपुरुष (the deity supporting the building to be built on the site chosen for a temple or a होउसे).
Paṭala 12 (46 verses)
Aṅkurārpaṇa or sowing of some seeds in the site chosen for construction is the subject discussed here.
Paṭala 13 (76 verses)
This section is devoted to describing the various processes involved in मन्त्र-दीक्षा or ceremonially imparting a मन्त्र to a worthy disciple.
Paṭala 14 (264 verses)
This paṭala deals with 32 kinds of Vedic fires. Similarly Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Kāmya fire-rituals also have been portrayed here.
Thus ends the Sāmānyapāda here.
2. Mantrapāda
Paṭala 15 (136 verses)
This chapter is concerned with शिव transformed as Gaṇapati—called Prapañca- gaṇapati—and manifesting in six forms such as Āmoda and Pramoda, along with the respective consorts like Siddhi and Kānti. Offerings of flowers, fruits and the sweet modaka are also mentioned.
Paṭala 16 (127 verses)
This describes the following aspects of गणपति: Mahāgaṇapati, Siddhivināyaka, Kṣipragaṇapati and Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati.
The benefits of worshipping these are also given.
Paṭala 17 (98 verses)
Goddess पार्वती as Tripurā, meditation on her form, her मन्त्र and चक्र (yantra) and the benefits of her worship are delineated here.
Paṭala 18 (50 verses)
Vāgīśvarī in her three forms, viz., Haṁsavāgīśvarī, Daśākṣarī Vāgīśvarī and Siddhavāgīśvarī, is the subject discussed here.
Paṭala 19 (93 verses)
Called as Śrīhṛdayam, this chapter deals with the मन्त्र of लक्ष्मी which must be received from a preceptor.
The author has dealt with the subject in 34 different metres.
Paṭala 20 (38 verses)
This section too is dedicated to the goddess लक्ष्मी.
Metres used are 28.
Paṭala 21 (166 verses)
Christened as Śaktipaṭala this section deals with the different modes of worship of देवी or शक्ति ranging from the pleasant to horrible forms.
The number of metres used is 30.
Paṭala 22 (80 verses)
Goddess Tvaritā (like a hunter-woman) is the deity described here.
Ten metres are used in this section.
Paṭala 23 (77 verses)
Different aspects of मोथेर्-goddess like Nityaklinnā and Vajraprastāriṇī as also गौरी are described here.
Number of metres used is 19.
Paṭala 24 (85 verses)
Since it covers the worship of five aspects of the goddess दुर्गा it is called Pañcadurgā-paṭala.
Meters used are 10 in number.
Paṭala 25 (87 verses)
Two aspects of the Divine मोथेर्, वनदुर्गा and Śūlinī are dealt with here.
Twelve metres have been used.
Paṭala 26 (128 verses)
Special mantras like Bhūhṛdaya, some more aspects of the goddess like Tripuṭā and अन्नपूर्णा as also the rites to propitiate them are described here.
Eight metres have been used here.
Paṭala 27 (115 verses)
This paṭala, devoted to सूर्य, the Sun god gives his mudrās, mantras and modes of worship.
Paṭala 28 (164 verses)
Six Śaivamantras (mantras of शिव) are given here.
Paṭala 29 (101 verses)
This section gives the mantras concerning the three aspects of शिव, viz., Mṛtyuñ- जय, Tryambaka and दक्षिणामूर्ति.
Paṭala 30 (127 verses)
The Aghoramantra and the Aghora-śastra of शिव, are described here. They are effective in curing the diseases of human beings and animals.
Paṭala 31 (150 verses)
Some mantras of शिव and several conceptions of सुब्रह्मण्य are dealt with here.
Paṭala 32 (160 verses)
This paṭala contains the mantras of several deities such as शास्ता, क्षेत्रपाल, चण्डेश्वर, इन्द्र and some Yakṣas, as also the results obtained by propitiating these.
Paṭala 33 (132 verses)
The Aṣṭākṣarīmantra, the most effective of all the Vaiṣṇava mantras, is given here.
Paṭala 34 (92 verses)
Śrīkarāṣṭākṣaramantra of विष्णु and Gopālakamantra of Kṛṇā are described here.
Paṭala 35 (180 verses)
This section is devoted to Nṛhari or नरसिṁह and his मन्त्र.
Paṭala 36 (43 verses)
Two mantras of Varāha (the boar इन्चर्नतिओन्), the Mahāvarāha and the Varāhaikākṣara are given here.
Paṭala 37 (108 verses)
The superhuman form of सुदर्शन (the disc of विष्णु) and his मन्त्र as also the यन्त्र are dealt with here.
Paṭala 38 (101 verses)
The Trailokyamohanamantra pertaining to वामन (the dwarf इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) and the associated rites are described here.
Paṭala 39 (166 verses)
Mantras to be used for curing a person bitten by snakes are described here.
Paṭala 40 (174 verses)
Treatment for the poison injected by different creatures like serpents, scorpions, rats, spiders and mad dogs is given here showing the knowledge of toxicology of the author.
Paṭala 41 (111 verses)
Treatment of children afflicted by evil spirits or diseases like convulsions is described here.
Paṭala 42 (36 verses)
This section deals with grahaceṣṭā or seizure by demonic forces which are 18 in number and the remedial measures.
Paṭala 43 (91 verses)
Bhūtabādhā or demoniac possession and its remedies using special mantras like Khaḍgarāvaṇa, Śūlinī and Vanadurgā are delineated here.
Paṭala 44 (24 verses)
Apasmāra or epilepsy and its cure by certain medicines is described here.
Paṭala 45 (207 verses)
Fevers of eight kinds—classified as Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva!—and some other common diseases are dealt with in this section along with the remedial mantras and medicines.
Paṭala 46 (148 verses)
Diseases of the eye, nose, throat, ear, head etc., are the topics discussed here.
Paṭala 47 (130 verses)
Ṣaṭkarmas—See ṢAṬKARMAS.—or the six sorcerous rites and Yama-mantra are described here. They should be used only against the criminals and enemies of the society.
Paṭala 48 (105 verses)
Subjugation by enchantment, called ākṛṣṭi, with Lavaṇamantra is the subject of this paṭala.
Paṭala 49 (15 verses)
This small section deals with the diseases of cows and their cure with medicines as also mantras.
Paṭala 50 (51 verses)
Preparation of certain substances like asafoetida and camphor oil is described here.
Paṭala 51 (75 verses)
Amusement by creating delusions and jugglery are the subject matter.
Paṭala 52 (163 verses)
Methods of knowing about victory in a battle through the auguries connected with five birds and the rites to be performed to ensure victory are given here.
3. Kriyāpāda
Paṭala 1 (161 verses)
This paṭala deals with four topics: Śivasadbhāva (existence of शिव); Āgama-prāmāṇya (authenticity of the आगमस्); Tattvamātṛkā (letters of the alphabet as aspects of the Divine मोथेर्; and Vastunirdeśa (36 tattvas or fundamental principles of शैवागमस्).
Paṭala 2 (40 verses)
This section discusses the six well-known categories of the शैवागमस् and criticises the views of other schools.
Paṭala 3 (127 verses)
The नित्यकर्म or the daily routine of a religious man is discussed here in great detail.
Paṭala 4 (43 verses)
This describes the purification of the body by स्नान or bath and that of the मिन्द् by योग.
Paṭala 5 (140 verses)
This paṭala deals with the उपचारस् or modes of ritualistic worship of deities which may be 16 or 10 or 5
Paṭala 6 (131 verses)
The six major aspects of a tāntrik rite are described here. They are: मन्त्र (sacred formula); मुद्रा (poses of fingers and hand); kuṇḍa (pit for establishing the sacred fire); मण्डल (esoteric diagram); द्रव्य (specific substances to be used in the rite); and the sādhaka (performer of the rite).
Paṭala 7 (18 verses)
Several mudrās or poses of fingers and hand are stated here.
Paṭala 8 (133 verses)
Kuṇḍas (sacrificial pits) of various types and maṇḍalas (esoteric diagrams) of various colours are given in great detail in this section.
Paṭala 9 (29 verses)
Details of the vessels and materials used in sacrifices, such as sruk and sruva (wooden spoons), araṇis (wooden pieces for producing fire), इध्म (fuel-sticks) are provided here.
Paṭala 10 (51 verses)
The subject of this paṭala is दीक्षा (taking certain vows on an auspicious day) before beginning a rite. अङ्कुरार्पण (sowing of certain seeds for the protection of the rite) (See AṄKURĀRPAṆA for details.) which is an important aspect of many religious rites is also described here.
Paṭala 11 (20 verses)
Qualities of the आचार्य (chief priest) who can officiate in the rites, as also of his disciples or assistants are enumerated here.
Paṭala 12 (104 verses)
Attendant deities like नवग्रहस्, गणपति, द्वारपालस् and Saptamātṛkās—their forms and worship—are the subject matter here.
Paṭala 13 (172 verses)
The rituals for the worship of शिव are elaborated in this paṭala.
Paṭala 14 (32 verses)
Worship of शिव with five faces—called Pañcāvaraṇa—is the main topic discussed here.
Paṭala 15
This paṭala is in prose. It enumerates the proceedings of the daily sacrifice to be performed according to the शैवागमस्.
Paṭala 16 (81 verses)
Śivadīkṣā has two aspects: Sabīja and Nirbīja. The latter meant for ordinary persons, has four varieties. This has been discussed here.
Paṭala 17 (231 verses)
Six adhvās or paths such as Tattva, वर्ण and मन्त्र are described in detail for the benefit of the priest. Each of these has several subdivisions.
Paṭala 18 (134 verses)
Nirvāṇadīkṣā to be given by the preceptor to a worthy disciple is explained here in great detail. A considerable part of this section is in prose.
Paṭala 19 (90 verses)
Sādhakadīkṣā—sādhaka means the priest here—the ceremonial vow to be taken by the priest of the sacrifice is described here with all the details, both in verses and in prose.
Paṭala 20 (38 verses)
This short section deals with the prāyaścittas or expiatory rites to ward off the evil effects of mistakes committed in the performance of the rites.
Paṭala 21 (127 verses)
Pavitrāropaṇa, investing the image in the sanctum of the temple, with the यज्ञोपवीत or the sacred thread, once a year is the subject discussed here.
Paṭala 22 (71 verses)
Worship of the creeper damana (artemisia indica) during Vasanta or the spring season is described here. It is said to please शिव.
Paṭala 23 (41 verses)
For performing sacrifices and constructing temples, the land should be carefully selected as per the rules prescribed by competent authorities. That is being explained here.
Paṭala 24 (35 verses)
As a prelude to architectural designs the author introduces certain measurements in this chapter, based on the shadow of a Śaṅku or gnomon. This is called ‘Śaṅkucchāyā’.
Paṭala 25 (85 verses)
Technical terms for the measurement of lands as also the definition of places like villages, towns and cities etc., are discussed and stated here.
Paṭala 26 (126 verses)
Selecting a suitable land for building a temple and making it ready is described here.
Paṭala 27 (105 verses)
Vāstupūjā (worship of the वास्तुपुरुष), iṣṭakānyāsa (installation of bricks) and fixing the place for the गर्भगृह (sanctum) are the topics dealt with in this paṭala.
Paṭala 28 (145 verses)
The description and enumeration of temples and dwellings of men is the chief topic of this section wherein 52 varieties of temples and 46 varieties of dwellings for men have been described.
Paṭala 29 (217 verses)
The same topic of the previous paṭala is continued here, giving details.
Paṭala 30 (79 verses)
Several types of structures for the dwelling of human beings are described here. Multi-storeyed buildings (from 3 storeys up to 12) also can be built. However, buildings higher than 100 hastas (about 150 feet) are not safe and hence should not be attempted.
Paṭala 31 (149 verses)
This chapter is devoted to the enume-ration and description of the different parts of a temple like base, pillars, rafters, beams and doors. Several varieties of each are also mentioned based upon the works of मय and पराशर.
Paṭala 32 (124 verses)
Several architectural details of the temple structure are given here. Construction of a big water tank for the benefit of weary travellers is also dealt with.
Paṭala 33 (101 verses)
Six types of materials like granite, wood and baked bricks, needed for the construction of temples and palaces are dealt with in detail.
Paṭala 34 (94 verses)
This paṭala discusses the topic of the selection of a well-qualified स्थपति or architect and the fixing of the pinnacle (stūpī and kumbha) under his guidance. Other topics delineated are the installation of the idol on an auspicious day and allied subjects.
Paṭala 35 (120 verses)
Repair of damaged parts of a temple, places of minor deities and details of the गोपुर (ornamental tower in front of the main gate) are the subjects dealt with here.
Paṭala 36 (80 verses)
Types of idols—without form, with definite forms and with a partial form as also the materials used to make them are described here.
Paṭala 37 (82 verses)
This section describes the selection of granite by applying various methods of testing.
Paṭala 38 (59 verses)
Measurements and others details connected with the preparation of इदोल्स् are taken up here. The three forms of temple architecture viz., नागर, द्राविड and वेसर are also discussed.
Paṭala 39 (105 verses)
Twelve varieties of pīṭhas or bases of images are described in this paṭala.
Paṭala 40 (38 verses)
Idols made of different materials, prepared according to the specifications of शैवागमस्, form the subject matter.
Paṭala 41 (131 verses)
Idols of three types—acala (fixed), cala (movable) and calācala (movable and fixed)—are discussed here. Details of measurements of the images of male deities are also given.
Paṭala 42 (84 verses)
Measurements concerning the इदोल्स् of female deities are given in this paṭala.
Paṭala 43 (118 verses)
In this section 16 forms of शिव associated with पार्वती and स्कन्द, and other aspects, are described along with the weapons and the mount नन्दि.
Paṭala 44 (28 verses)
Purificatory rites in a temple after the installation ceremony are the main topic discussed.
Paṭala 45 (117 verses)
Rites connected with the installation of the idol, including refixing after repair works are detailed here.
Paṭala 46 (109 verses)
Infusing life into the image after ceremonially bathing it with waters drawn from several sacred rivers is the main subject dealt with here.
Paṭala 47 (134 verses)
Rites in connection with the installa-tion are detailed again in this section.
Paṭala 48 (107 verses)
Nityotsava or the daily rituals of the temples is the main topic here. Annual festivals are also discussed.
Paṭala 49 (238 verses)
Observance of occasional festivals as also dhvajārohaṇa (hoisting the temple flag) are described in this paṭala.
Paṭala 50 (368 verses)
This long chapter deals mainly with the bathing of the image with sanctified water from numerous pots, the number of pots varying from 9 up to 1008.
Paṭala 51 (71 verses)
Installation of the इदोल्स् of gods like सूर्य, गणपति, स्कन्द, दुर्गा and others is the topic of this paṭala. The worship of सूर्य is dealt with in great detail.
Paṭala 52 (46 verses)
This chapter is devoted to the installation and worship of Vighneśvara or गणेश.
Paṭala 53 (93 verses)
Installation and worship of स्कन्द is the topic here.
Paṭala 54 (148 verses)
Installation of Haranārāyaṇa or शङ्करनारायण and his worship are described here.
Paṭala 55 (91 verses)
This section is devoted to the installa-tion and worship of मोथेर् दुर्गा.
Paṭala 56 (101 verses)
Gaurī is the goddess whose installation and worship are discussed here.
Paṭala 57 (87 verses)
Goddess सरस्वती is the main topic of this chapter.
Paṭala 58 (84 verses)
Śāstā or Bhūtanātha is the topic discussed here. Measurements of the idol, details of the weapons and his eight aspects like Goptā, Piṅgala and Vīrasena are also described.
Paṭala 59 (168 verses)
The सप्तमातृकास् (Seven Divine Mothers) such as ब्राह्मी, Māheśvarī and कौमारी as also वीरभद्र and Vighneśvara, always go together in temples. Their installation and associated rituals have been described here.
Paṭala 60 (85 verses)
Every temple must have a क्षेत्रपाल to protect the sanctum. His installation and other details are given here.
Paṭala 61 (56 verses)
The method of offering ड़ोओद् to the deity in a temple prepared out of grains after the harvest is described here. Festival of lamps conducted during special occasions is also narrated.
Paṭala 62 (94 verses)
Antyeṣṭi or ड़ुनेरल् रितेस् are described here in great detail.
Large portions of this section are in prose and poetry, but un-numbered.
Paṭala 63 (101 verses)
Prāyaścittas or expiatory rites are the main topic discussed here.
Paṭala 64 (52 verses)
Renovation of the इदोल्स्, shrines and other structures forms the main topic.
Thus ends the Kriyāpāda here.
4. Yogapāda
Paṭala 1 (55 verses)
In this paṭala characteristics of Yoga—the means to मोक्ष or liberation—with वैराग्य or the spirit of renunciation as the chief means, are described.
This Yogapāda is the shortest and has just 3 paṭalas.
Paṭala 2 (87 verses)
The concept of योग, based on the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि, is explained here including the first four steps of the eight-limbed योग.
Paṭala 3 (96 verses)
Starting again with प्राणायाम the last four steps have been covered here.
Epilogue
The original work in देवनागरी script, based on three manuscripts, was first edited and published by T. गणपति Śāstri in A.

from Trivandrum (now Tiruvananthapuram). Due to the defects in the manuscripts, a small part of the text has been lost. Quite a large portion is in prose. This part as also many verses have not been numbered. Hence it can be said that the work contains more material than the 18,000 verses mentioned earlier.
The style of the work is simple and elegant. The material presented is very vast and covers several fields of ancient and medieval knowledge.
Though some portions seem to reflect the culture of Kerala region of India more, the relevance of the work as a whole to the field of Hindu rituals cannot be questioned.
It is a treat for the scholars of Indology in general and to the Hindu priestly class in particular.
See also HINDU TEMPLES, MŪRTIŚILPA-ŚĀSTRA and TANTRAS.

Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Out of the six systems of philosophy of orthodox हिन्दुइस्म्, the Vedānta system is the most popular one. Its canonical works are: the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahma-sūtras and the Bhagavadgītā.
Though the total number of उपनिषद्स् available in print today, exceeds 250, only ten out of them have been universally accepted as basic and authoritative, since शङ्कर (A.

-820), the earliest commentator, has chosen to write commentaries only on these ten. As he has quoted from another three or four more उपनिषद्स्, these too have been recognized as ancient and authentic texts.
The Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad—also spelt as Īśopaniṣad—is the first in this list. It gets this appellation since it begins with the word ‘īśāvāsyam.’ It is sometimes christened as Saṁhitopaniṣad also, since—as a lone exception—it appears in the Saṁhitā portion of the Śukla Yajurveda (as its 40th chapter), also called the Vājasaneyī Saṁhitā. Though a short work of only 18 verses, it has attracted the attention of many a scholar, resulting in the maximum number of Sanskrit commentaries on any single Upaniṣad. And, in spite of the strenuous efforts of these intellectual giants, the Upaniṣad continues to baffle the reader even today!
The first verse declares that the whole world is permeated by God—called Īśa here—and advises the human beings to enjoy it in a spirit of detachment since it belongs to God and not to them. Consequently greed for others’ wealth and possessions is forbidden.
The second verse advises all human beings to aspire to live for a hundred years but spend that life in working for the welfare—both temporal and spiritual—of the world. If life is spent in this way, कर्म or action can never taint and be a cause for suffering.
If on the other hand, this advice is not heeded, such transgressors—declares the third verse—will have to suffer in dark hellish worlds!
The next two verses describe, though in an enigmatic language, the nature of the आत्मन्, the inner and the true Self of all.
Verses 6 and 7, portray the state attained by a person who has realized this आत्मन्. Since he perceives the same universal Spirit in all, he loves all, thus transcending hatred, delusion and sorrow which are always caused by the seeing of duality.
The next, the 8th, verse gives a highly poetical description of this आत्मन् in its universal dimension, as all-pervading, effulgent, absolutely pure and as the Supreme Ruler.
The next six verses (9 to 14) have proved to be rather obscure and the traditional commentators have differed widely in their interpretations.
The wise ones declare that the end results of विद्या and अविद्या are entirely different. However, a balanced combination of these two alone can lead to इम्मोर्तलित्य्.
‘Avidyā’ has been interpreted as Vedic rituals, and ‘vidyā’ as the upāsanās (meditations) on the Vedic deities preceded by a ज्ञान (knowledge) about them. Mere Vedic rituals will lead to पितृलोक (the world of manes) and mere upāsanās on the Vedic gods, to devaloka (heaven). But one has to return to this world from both of them, after exhausting the religious merit. Since a taste of the pleasures of these worlds creates a strong tendency in one’s psyche to try for them again, the person takes recourse to the same course—Vedic rituals for getting to पितृलोक or Vedic meditations to attain devaloka—thereby missing the royal path that leads to मुक्ति or freedom from transmigratory existence. It is this spiritual tragedy that has been described by the Upaniṣad as ‘entering into blinding darkness’ (andhaṁ tamaḥ).
When a balanced combination of these two is practised, in the right spirit, the result will be entirely different. Performance of Vedic rituals and ordained duties of one’s life will lead to the purification of the मिन्द्. meditation on God (Īśa) practised by such a pure मिन्द् will lead ultimately to realising him, resulting in मोक्ष (liberation or इम्मोर्तलित्य्).
Opinions of the commentators seem to be even more sharply divided with regard to the words sambhūti, asambhūti and vināśa, used in the verses 12 to 14.
Śaṅkara takes the words sambhūti and asambhūti to mean the Kāryabrahma (or हिरण्यगर्भ, the totality of च्रेअतिओन्, the First in evolution) and the कारण-brahma (Prakṛti or Avyākṛta, the subtle causal state before च्रेअतिओन्) respectively. meditation on the former leads to the acquisition of the supernatural psychic powers and on the latter, to a state called ‘prakṛtilaya,’ a state in which the सोउल् lies merged in प्रकृति, in a state of apparent stupor, free from all experiences of joy or sorrow. (c. f. Yogasūtras 1.19 of पतञ्जलि.) The former leads one astray from the spiritual path whereas the latter resembles inertness and consequently no effort is made in any direction.
Since both these results—from the standpoint of मोक्ष or ultimate liberation—lead one away from the spiritual goal, they have been termed ‘andhaṁ tamaḥ’ or blinding darkness.
An interesting interpretation—which appears to be more convincing or reasonable—has been offered by Uvaṭācārya (11th century), the commentator on the Mādhyandina recension of the Śukla Yajurveda. According to him, sambhūti is परब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) and vināśa (= asambhūti) is the body. Since continual hunger and thirst result in the death of the physical body which is an invaluable instrument of sādhanā (spiritual effort), they have to be transcended by suitable secular activities. Then, through contemplation on ब्रह्मन्, one can attain इम्मोर्तलित्य्. That is why a balanced combination of both is needed.
The verses 15 to 18 describe the prayers addressed to God, in and through the orb of the sun, by the earnest spiritual seeker who is on his deathbed.
In the verse 15, he requests God to remove the obstacle to his vision, the obstacle being the attractions of this material world which have hidden God’s glorious face. In the next verse the same prayer is continued with a description of God’s attributes and a hint of the experience of identity of the aspirant with him.
In the verse 17, the aspirant, becoming aware of the imminent death of the body prays to अग्नि, the presiding deity of his sacrificial fire—or the word ‘kratu’ here may mean God himself—to remember his good deeds and save him.
In the last verse, the 18th, he urges अग्नि to take him to ब्रह्मलोक or सत्य-लोक from which there is no return to mundane existence, by the arcirādimārga or देवयान, the path of light, believed to be leading the spiritually mature souls to that world.
At a time when there seems to have been a conflict between the concepts of work and worship, and, some sages were laying a greater emphasis on renunciation and monastic way of life, the teachings of this Upaniṣad must have come as a refreshing contrast for the ordinary, but earnest, sādhakas. Giving up selfish and desire-motivated actions, performing acts of charity and service, devotion to God and considering human life more as a blessing than as a curse, are the central messages of this small but beautiful Upaniṣad.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Īśāna
(‘One who rules’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, the third deity of the Hindu Trinity, has several aspects. As Pañcā-nana, he is represented as a five-faced god, of which ईशान is the first face turned towards the Zenith. He represents the highest aspect and is also called ‘Sadāśiva’. On the physical plane he represents the power that rules over आकाश or ether, the sky. On the spiritual plane he is the deity that grants मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Īśāna is also the name of one of the eight दिक्पालकस्, the guardian-deities of the quarters, the north-east being the direction assigned to him.
He is also classed among the eleven Rudras of the Vedic pantheon, representing the principles of प्राण or life-force.
Sometimes, the Rudras are listed as eight and ईशान is one of them. Actually all these are different names of शिव himself.
Iconographical works represent him as शिव in the human form, with four hands, in one of which he is holding the trident and is riding a bull. Īśānī is his consort. She is the same as पार्वती.
